title: std::thread, jthread and Shared State
objectives: Create, join and detach std::thread objects, and explain why an unjoined joinable thread is a bug
Define a data race precisely and identify unsafe shared-state patterns (reference capture, reads before join)
Use std::jthread (C++20) with std::stop_token for cooperative, RAII-safe cancellation
Classify what is legal to share between threads: immutable data, thread-local data, or synchronised data
motivation: A feed handler decodes packets while another thread rebuilds the order book and a third recomputes risk: concurrency is how market-data systems meet deadlines without serialising every call. But the moment two threads touch the same bytes without synchronisation, the program has undefined behaviour, not a crash you can debug, but a licence to print nonsense prices. This lesson builds the vocabulary, threads, join, shared state, data races, that every later lesson on locks, atomics and lock-free code depends on.

blocks.text: Threads: one address space, many instruction pointers

blocks.md: A **thread** is an independent stream of instructions: its own stack, registers and program counter. Unlike processes, all threads of a program share one address space, the heap, globals and open files. That sharing is the whole point: passing a pointer between threads costs nothing, which is why threads are the unit of concurrency in low-latency systems. It is also the danger: any shared byte can be reached by any thread at any time.

Distinguish **concurrency** (tasks overlap, possibly by interleaving on one core) from **parallelism** (tasks run simultaneously on multiple cores). `std::thread` gives you both opportunistically: the scheduler decides. What C++ guarantees is the memory model, which effects are visible to which thread, given the synchronisation you perform. Everything else (cores, affinity, preemption) is platform detail that later low-latency lessons cover.

blocks.caption: Threads do not get their own memory objects: two threads' pointers can land on the same 4 bytes. Cheap sharing, and the source of every data race.

blocks.md: `std::thread` starts a callable immediately. A thread object is **joinable** until you call `join()` (main waits for completion) or `detach()` (the thread runs on, unowned). Destroying a joinable `std::thread` calls `std::terminate()` - there is no implicit join, so `std::thread` alone is not RAII-safe.

blocks.caption: join() is also a synchronisation point: everything a worker did before returning is visible to main after join().

blocks.title: std::thread is not RAII (until C++20)
blocks.md: An exception thrown between construction and `join()` still destroys a joinable thread, and terminates the program. `std::jthread` (C++20) fixes the lifecycle: its destructor **requests stop** and **joins**, and it takes a `std::stop_token` for cooperative cancellation. On a C++17 baseline, wrap `std::thread` in your own RAII class.

blocks.caption: Labelled C++20: stop_token makes cancellation explicit instead of a boolean you race on.

blocks.md: A **data race** is precisely: two or more threads access the same memory location, **at least one access is a write**, and the accesses are not ordered by synchronisation. The consequence is not "the slower write wins", it is **undefined behaviour**: the compiler may assume no races exist, cache values in registers, vectorise reads, and reorder stores. "Benign race" is a myth; races on non-atomic types have no defined outcome at all.

blocks.caption: ++counter is three steps, load, add, store, and threads interleave inside those steps. This program is undefined, not merely inaccurate.

blocks.md: So what *is* safe to share? Exactly three options: **immutable data** (written before threads start, then never written again - `const` makes the intent enforceable), **thread-local data** (`thread_local` gives each thread its own instance), and **synchronised data**, where every conflicting access is ordered by join, a mutex, or an atomic operation. The rest of this module is about building that third option correctly.

items: Before sharing `X`, answer: **who writes it, who reads it, and what orders them?** If any answer is "nobody yet", you are writing a race.
Passing locals by reference into a thread that outlives the frame is a second, quieter bug: dangling references, even without a race.
`std::thread::hardware_concurrency()` gives a hint about core count, it is guidance for pool sizing, never a synchronisation tool.

blocks.title: Why the desk cares
blocks.md: A book-builder thread writes the order book while a pricing thread reads it. An unsynchronised read may see a half-updated book, a bid without its ask, and quote nonsense prices. There is no crash, no log line, just silently wrong markets until someone reconciles positions. Race vocabulary is risk vocabulary.

guidedExercise.prompt: Write a program that sums a `std::vector<double>` of 1,000,000 elements using 4 threads, each summing one contiguous quarter and writing its partial result into `partial[q]` of a pre-sized `std::vector<double>`. Join all threads, then print the total. Then answer: why is `partial[q] = s` from four threads not a data race, while a single shared running total would be?
hints: `partial.resize(4)` before starting the threads, each thread writes only its own element, a distinct memory location.
A data race needs two threads reaching the *same* location with a write; distinct elements never conflict.
The join calls create the happens-before edges that make main's final reads safe.

independentExercise.prompt: A colleague's function contains: `std::thread t(load_prices, std::ref(buf)); std::cout << buf[0]; ... return;` (so `t` goes out of scope joined-unjoined). Identify **two** distinct bugs by name and mechanism, then rewrite the function so both disappear, once with an explicit `join()` and once with `std::jthread` (C++20).
hints: Bug one fires at scope exit, before any output even prints, if `t` is still joinable.
Bug two fires at the `cout`: reading `buf` races with the loader's writes because nothing orders them.
`join()` before reading orders the accesses; `std::jthread` additionally fixes the scope-exit bug automatically.

commonMistakes: Letting a joinable `std::thread` be destroyed, this is `std::terminate()`, not an implicit join.
Detaching a thread "to avoid the join", then reading the data it touches: detach removes the only synchronisation point you had.
Capturing local variables by reference in a thread lambda that outlives the function's stack frame.
Treating a race as harmless because outputs "usually look right", undefined behaviour has no usual.
Assuming `++x` is atomic because it is one line of source; it is load-add-store, three operations a thread can interleave with.
realWorldApplication: Every production trading system is multi-threaded: feed handlers decode, book builders update, risk engines price. Correct thread lifecycle and race identification is the entry ticket; getting it wrong shows up as corrupt state, not crashes.
quantFinanceApplication: The book-builder/pricing-thread split in this lesson's callout is the canonical shared-state design: one writer thread updates the order book, reader threads consume it, and the entire correctness story is the synchronisation between them, exactly what the rest of this module formalises.
summary: Threads share one address space while keeping private stacks and registers: cheap communication, expensive mistakes.
A joinable `std::thread` must be joined or detached before destruction; destroying it while joinable calls `std::terminate()`. `std::jthread` (C++20) requests stop and joins in its destructor.
A data race is concurrent, unsynchronised access to one memory location with at least one write, and it is undefined behaviour in C++.
The only safe sharing is immutable data, thread-local data, or data ordered by synchronisation (join, mutex, atomics).
`join()` is more than waiting: it creates the happens-before edge that makes a worker's writes visible to the joining thread.

quiz.prompt: What happens when a still-joinable `std::thread` object is destroyed?
options: The destructor joins the thread automatically
The thread is detached and leaks
quiz.explanation: `std::thread`'s destructor terminates the program if the thread is joinable, no implicit join, no exception. `std::jthread` (C++20) is the type that joins on destruction.

quiz.prompt: What does this program print (think about what join() guarantees)?
quiz.explanation: The lambda's write to `x` happens-before main's read because `t.join()` synchronises the two threads. The output is deterministic: 7.

quiz.prompt: Which of these are valid operations on a joinable `std::thread t;` (assume another thread object exists where needed)?
quiz.explanation: `std::thread` is movable but not copyable, copy assignment/construction is a compile error. join() and detach() are the two lifecycle operations.

quiz.prompt: Define a data race precisely, in one or two sentences.
quiz.modelAnswer: Two or more threads access the same memory location concurrently, at least one access is a write, and the accesses are not ordered by synchronisation. In C++ this is undefined behaviour.
quiz.explanation: The definition has three clauses, same location, at least one write, no ordering, and the consequence is UB, not 'last write wins'.

quiz.prompt: Which construct both waits for a worker to finish AND guarantees its writes are visible to the waiting thread?
quiz.explanation: `join()` creates a happens-before edge: all writes sequenced before the worker's return are visible afterwards. Sleeping is timing luck; volatile does not provide inter-thread ordering; hardware_concurrency() reports core count.

quiz.prompt: What does the destructor of a C++20 std::jthread do if the thread is still joinable (labelled C++20)?
options: Requests stop, then joins the thread
Throws if the thread has not finished
quiz.explanation: jthread's destructor calls request_stop() (if a stop source exists) and join(), making the type RAII-safe, the standard fix for lesson's terminate-at-scope-exit trap.

flashcards.front: What exactly is a data race in C++?
flashcards.back: Two+ threads access the same memory location, at least one access is a write, and no synchronisation orders the accesses. Consequence: undefined behaviour.
join(): caller blocks until the thread finishes and gets a happens-before edge on its writes. detach(): ownership is released; no synchronisation, no way to wait, almost never what you want.

flashcards.front: Why is std::thread not RAII-safe, and what fixes it?
flashcards.back: Destroying a joinable thread calls std::terminate(). std::jthread (C++20) requests stop and joins in its destructor; on C++17 you write your own scope-guard wrapper.

flashcards.front: int x = 1; std::thread t([&x]{ x = 7; }); t.join(); std::cout << x;: what prints?
flashcards.back: 7, join() synchronises the lambda's write with the read; the output is deterministic.

flashcards.front: Name the three safe ways to share data between threads.
flashcards.back: Immutability (write once before threads start), thread_local storage (private copies), or explicit synchronisation (join, mutex, atomics) on every conflicting access.
